newsitem.title: CANADA: OECD sees 3.5 pct GDP growth in Canada in 1997.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees 3.5 pct GDP growth in Canada in 1997.

text.p: Surging household and business demand in Canada suggests the Canadian economy has room for strong growth without inflation, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said in a report released on Thursday.

The OECD saw gross domestic product at market prices growing by 3.5 percent in 1997 and by 3.3 percent in 1998. The projection was an increase from the organization's earlier projections of 3.3 percent growth for 1997.
GDP growth in Canada in 1996 was 1.5 percent.
But the OECD said unemployment in Canada was expected to decline only slowly, to 9.4 percent in 1997 and 9.1 percent in 1998, down from an average of 9.7 percent in 1996.
"The acceleration in economic activity has not yet been reflected in the labor market," the OECD said.
"Unemployment is projected to decline only gradually, remaining above its estimated structural rate."
The slack in Canada's economy meant there was little risk of inflation, the agency said.

"Given the sizeable slack in product and labor markets, the economy should have room for strong, above-potential rates of growth in output and employment in coming quarters, without a resurgence of inflation," the report said.
The report also projected that Canadian federal and provincial budgets would have a "significant surplus" by 1998 on a national accounts basis.
The agency said Canada's external current account was unlikely to improve further because of stronger import growth, but was expected to remain in broad balance.

The OECD said, however, that the recent spurt in household demand could be short-lived, given continuing fiscal drag, relatively high personal debt levels, a historically low saving ratio, high unemployment and strill fragile consumer confidence.

The OECD said a second risk to the Canadian outlook was possible monetary tightening in the United States, which could pressure Canadian rates even if domestic conditions did not warrant tighter conditions in Canada.
